INTRODUCTION
 
            I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science & Technology,
 Environment & Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this One
 Hundred Sixty-first Report of the Committee. This Report deals with the detailed Demands for Grants (2006-2007) of
 the Department of Space (Demand No.88).
 
2.         In the meeting of the Committee held on the 4
th  April, 2006 the Secretary and other Officers of the Department
 of Space gave an overview of the various activities of the Department and the Members sought clarifications on various
 aspects of the performance of the Department to enable it to scrutinise the Demands for Grants.
 
3.         The Committee expresses its thanks to the Officers of the Department for replying to the clarifications sought by
 the Members and placing before it the required material to enable the Committee to scrutinise the Demands for Grants
 of the Department of Space.
 
4.         The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on the 15
th May, 2006.
NEW DELHI;  
May  15, 2006
P. G. NARAYANAN,   
    Chairman
Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee
 on  Science & Technology, Environment & Forests.
 
 
REPORT
The Indian Space programme is characterised by a vision to use space technology for the socio-economic benefit of the
 nation through establishment of operational space services in a self-reliant manner. Over the last three decades, India
 has achieved notable progress in the design, development and operation of space systems, as well as, using them for
 vital services like telecommunication, television broadcasting, meteorology, disaster warning and natural resources
 survey and management. The space programme has become largely self-reliant with capability to design and build
 satellites for providing space services and to launch them using indigenously designed and developed launch vehicles. 
2.         The primary objective of the Indian Space Programme is to promote the development and application of space

 technology and space science. The main thrust areas of the programme are:
Satellite-based communication for various applications;
Satellite-based resources survey and management and environmental monitoring;
Meteorological applications; and
Development and operationalisation of indigenous satellites, launch vehicles and associated ground segment for
 providing these space-based services.
3.         The Space Commission and the Department of Space (DOS) were set-up by the  Government of India in the year
 1972. DOS is responsible for implementing the policies framed by the Space Commission.  These are carried out
 through the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) and the Grant-in-aid institutions viz., National Remote Sensing
 Agency (NRSA), Physical Research Laboratory (PRL), National Atmospheric Research Laboratory (NARL), North-
Eastern Space Applications Centre (NE-SAC) and Semi-Conductors Laboratory (SCL).
4.         The Secretariat of Department of Space and the Headquarters of ISRO are located in Bangalore. Programme
 Offices at ISRO Headquarters co-ordinate the overall programmes like satellite communication, earth observation,
 launch vehicle, space science, space industry development, disaster management support, international co-operation,
 publications and public relations, budget and economic analysis and human resource development.
The major Centres, Units and establishments of ISRO/DOS responsible for carrying out research and development
 activities as well as for undertaking various projects and programmes, are given below:
Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre (VSSC), Thiruvananthapuram, provides the technology base for the country’s
 indigenous launch vehicle (rocket) development.
Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre (LPSC), with its facilities at Bangalore, Thiruvananthapuram and Mahendragiri, is
 responsible for development of liquid propulsion and cryogenic propulsion systems for satellite and launch vehicles
Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC-SHAR) at Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh, is the launch base and  also, it provides the
 facilities for processing of solid rocket motors.
ISRO Satellite Centre (ISAC), Bangalore, is entrusted with the prime responsibility for the satellite development.  The
 Laboratory for Electro-Optics Systems (LEOS), Bangalore, of ISAC has the responsibility for development and
 productionisation of electro optical sensors for satellites.  ISRO Radar Development Unit (ISRAD), Bangalore of ISAC
 has the responsibility to develop the Radar systems for ISRO and other emerging radar systems for national
 development.
Space Applications Centre (SAC), Ahmedabad, carries out research and development in space applications as well as
 development of application payloads.
Development and Educational Communication Unit (DECU), Ahmedabad, is involved in the conception, definition,
 planning and socio/techno-economic evaluation of development communication programmes.
ISRO Telemetry, Tracking & Command Network (ISTRAC), with its ground stations at Bangalore, Sriharikota,
 Lucknow, Bearslake, Biak (Indonesia), Brunei and Mauritius provides the telemetry, tracking and command support
 and spacecraft mission management for the Indian remote sensing satellite missions, space science missions and
 satellite launch vehicle programmes.
INSAT Master Control Facility (MCF) at Hassan, Karnataka, has the responsibility for control and operation of INSAT
 satellites.
ISRO Inertial Systems Unit (IISU), Thiruvananthapuram, carries out research and development in the area of inertial
 systems for satellites and launch vehicles.
6.         A National Natural Resources Management System (NNRMS), with the  Department of Space (DOS) as the
 nodal agency, has been established to ensure optimal utilisation of natural resources using remote sensing data in
 conjunction with conventional techniques. Under NNRMS, five Regional Remote Sensing Service Centres (RRSSCs)
 at Bangalore, Dehradun, Jodhpur, Kharagpur and Nagpur have been set up for execution of remote sensing application
 programmes in the respective regions.      
7.         In addition to the aforesaid institutions, there are some Organisations receiving Grants-in-aid, under the
 Department of Space :
National Remote Sensing Agency (NRSA), Hyderabad, an autonomous institution, is responsible for acquisition,
 processing and dissemination of satellite and aerial remote sensing data.  The Indian Institute of Remote Sensing (IIRS)
 of NRSA, located at Dehradun imparts training in various disciplines to user scientists.
Physical Research Laboratory (PRL), Ahmedabad, an autonomous institution supported mainly by the Department of
 Space, carries out research in space sciences.
The National Atmospheric Research Laboratory (NARL) set up at Gadanki near Tirupati, conducts atmospheric
 research.

The Semi-conductor Complex Limited, a public sector enterprise, at Chandigarh has been transferred from the

8.         Apart from this, the Sponsored Research Programme(RESPOND) programme of ISRO supports sponsored
 research activity in space science, space applications and space technology in various national academic/research
 institutions and Space Technology Cells in premier technological institutes of the country through grants-in-aid.
 In addition to the above, there is a wholly-owned Government Company for marketing space products and services
 called the Antrix Corporation Limited, Bangalore, established in 1992.
BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
10.       The Committee has been informed that thePlanning Commission have fixed the Plan outlay for Department of
 Space at  Rs. 13,250 crores for the 10
th Five Year Plan. With the expected Non-Plan component of Rs. 2000 crores, the
 total outlay for 10th Plan would be Rs.15,250 crores. 
 
11.       The expenditure in the first three years of the Plan period has been Rs. 6965.37 crores  (Plan: Rs. 5988.26 Cr and
 Non-plan: Rs. 977.11 Cr) which is about 46% of the total approved  outlay.  Budget utilisation of more than 99% of the
 final approved grant has been maintained during the first three years of the plan period.
 
12.       The Committee has also been informed that the total expenditure during the 10
th Plan period would be Rs.
 13,251 crores approx including Plan and Non-plan components.  In respect of the Plan component, the 10th Plan
 expected expenditure would be Rs. 11,508 crores as against the target outlay of Rs. 13,250 crores. The shortfall of Rs.
 1742 crores under Plan is essentially due to savings in INSAT-4 costs, savings in Land/Civil works and Infrastructure
 operations cost and phasing out of expenditure on PSLV/GSLV Continuation and Earth Observation(EO) follow on
 missions based on programmatic schedules.  However, final picture on financial status of 10
th plan outlay would
 emerge during RE 2006-07, the last year of the 10th Five Year Plan.    
 
13.       The non-plan and plan break-up of the provision for BE  2006- 07 is as follows:

14.       In reply to a query as to whether the allocated funds are sufficient for carrying out the activities of the
 Department and whether any schemes / programmes are likely to be affected or discontinued, the Department clarified
 that for BE 2006-07 a projection of                      Rs. 4000 Crores was made and Rs 3610.42 Crores was allocated
 against it, which is as per the  programmatic requirements(Annexure) of all the ongoing projects/schemes and some of
 the new projects/schemes to be initiated in 2006-07. TheDepartment has reprioritised the requirement by phasing out
 expenditure on some of the new initiatives including Satellite Navigation in order to contain the budget during 2006-07
 within the allocated funds.
15.       In reply to another query of the Committee regarding the details of mechanism developed by the Department to
 monitor and review the progress of its ongoing schemes before formulating / finalising proposals for budgetary support,
 the Committee was apprised as follows:-
(i)         The proposals for annual budgetary support in the Department of Space are formulated under the frame work of
 the Decade Profile envisaged for 2001-10 and the Programmatic targets approved for the Tenth Five Year Plan 2002-
07. A detailed analysis of the programmatic accomplishments and specific targets for budgeting period is carried out
 while formulating the budget proposals.
(ii)           The Department has evolved a project management system wherein the progress of all the ongoing projects
 are reviewed by Project Management Boards / Management Councils before formulating their budget proposals.

INDIAN LUNAR MISSION - CHANDRAYAAN-1
17.       Chandrayaan-1 is India’s first scientific mission to Moon.  The main scientific objective of lunar mission is the
 physical and chemical maping of the moon from 100 km lunar polar orbit.  The mission life is 2 years.  The PSLV will
 place the lunar spacecraft in a 240 km X 24000 km orbit and the spacecraft will use its own propulsion system for
 reaching the 100 km orbit around the moon.  The total approved cost of Chandrayaan-1 is Rs. 386 Crores.
18.       In reply to a query regarding the allocation to the Indian Lunar Mission - Chandrayaan-1, which has been
 increased to Rs.142.75 Crores in 2006-07 as against Rs.106.22 Crores and Rs.60.00 Crores at BE and RE stages in
 2005-06, the Ministry explained that Chandrayaan-1 project has made significant progress. The configuration and
 design of the payloads and spacecraft has been completed and the establishment of Deep Space Network for receiving
 data from Chandrayaan-1 has progressed well. The project will be in hardware realisation phase in 2006-07. The
 increased allocation sought in 2006-07 is towards milestone payments for Deep Space Network, establishment of space
 science data centre, procurement of imaging payload components, spacecraft propulsion system components, solar cells
 and chemical cells, space qualified electronic components and electro-optic sensor's required for Chandrayaan satellite.
 Chandrayaan-1 is targeted for launch in 2007-08.
19.       On being asked about the advantages that the Americans and the Russians have gained subsequent to their moon
 project and what we will gain consequent to the Chandrayaan project,  the Secretary of the Department replied:-
“……….. the fact is Russians as well as Americans have collected samples from moon almost 20 years back.  That
 shows that they are well ahead of us in this field.  These missions were specifically related to some region on lunar
 surface.  Man landing on the moon was on a specific location.  They have collected some samples.  The Russians had
 robots there. They have conducted some experiments.  The entire surface of the moon has various mineralogical
 contents which will have to be assessed.  Even the Americans do not have the data with them. With these interests, a
 number of countries have come forward.  For example, Japanese, are going to launch a satellite to map moon, Chinese
 have similar plans.  Even there is renewed interest from   US to have the moon landing in the coming ten years or so. 
 So, there is a lot of interest created for the simple reason that minerals which are there.  There are two specific
 questions.  First, helium 3 whether is available in abundance.  Helium 3 is ideal for fusion reaction.  If we can get
 helium 3, it can become a big resource for us.  Second, whether there is water.  It is suspected to be available at various
 patches on moon.  This has to be explored.  Our mission is for exploration of such aspects.  More than that, this is a
 technology challenge of travelling long distances using rocket with the guided navigation system.  We are far ahead of
 other countries in space applications.  Third objective is to create enthusiasm among our scientists to explore the
 planetary science and planetary physics,  as you know, moon, which has been evolved from earth millions of years ago,
 studying moon will provide inputs on evolution of planet Earth.  That is why that will kindle scientific temperament. 
 We believe by this we can be in forefront for planetary exploration in the long run.  People are thinking of making the
 moon a base for exploration and mining of minerals and also a base for travel to other planets like Mars, etc. So, this is
 an investment towards future.”
20.       The Committee commends the role of the Indian space scientists in mastering a frontier space technology, which
 has brought the country close to the threshold of launching lunar spacecrafts and  hopes that the technologies developed
 in this mission would be fully exploited in the future for embarking on planetary missions with well thought out
 scientific objectives. The Committee also hopes that the mission would expand the scientific knowledge about the
 origin and evolution of moon, upgrade India’s space technological capabilities and provide challenging opportunities to
 the young scientists working in planetary sciences.
INDIAN REMOTE SENSING SATELLITES
21.       The Committee has been informed that India has established the National Natural Resources Management
 System (NNRMS) for which the Department of Space (DOS) is the nodal agency.  NNRMS is an integrated resource

 management system aimed at optimal utilisation of the country’s natural resources by a proper and systematic inventory
 of resource availability using remote sensing data in conjunction with conventional techniques.  The major elements of
 NNRMS encompass conceptualisation and implementation of space segments with the necessary ground-based date
 reception, processing and interpretation systems and integrating the satellite-based remotely sensed data with
 conventional data for resource management applications.
22.       The Indian Remote Sensing satellites form an important element of NNRMS for providing continuous remote
 sensing data services for the management of natural resources of the country.  A series of Indian Remote Sensing (IRS)
 satellites have been launched by India starting with IRS-1A in March 1988.  There are six remote sensing satellites in
 service at present –IRS-1C, IRS-P3, IRS-1D, OCEANSAT-1, TES and RESOURCESAT-1 – making IRS system the
 largest civilian remote sensing satellite constellation in the world. CARTOSAT-1is the latest satellite under IRS
 programme.
23.       The data from IRS satellites is utilised for several applications.  They include land use/cover mapping for agro-
climatic zones planning, wasteland mapping, forest cover mapping, Crop Acreage and Production Estimation, National
 River Action Plan for Sewerage Treatment Plants, Coastal Zone Regulation mapping, Integrated Mission for
 Sustainable Development, National (Natural) Resources Information System, etc.  In addition, different application
 studies of local/regional level are also being carried out by many organisations.  With high-resolution imageries of
 CARTOSAT-1, cadastral level applications will receive further impetus.
CARTOSAT-1
24.       CARTOSAT-1 is a state-of-the-art remote sensing satellite built by ISRO which is mainly intended for
 cartographic applications.  It is the eleventh satellite to be built in the Indian Remote Sensing (IRS) satellite series. 
 Weighing 1560 kg at lift-off, CARTOSAT-1 was launched into a 618 km high polar Sun Synchronous Orbit (SSO) by
 PSLV-C6 on               5
th  May, 2005.
25.       CARTOSAT-1 carries two state-of-the-art Panchromatic (PAN) cameras that take black and white stereoscopic
 pictures of the earth in the visible region of the electromagnetic spectrum.  The swath covered by these high resolution
 PAN cameras is 30 km and their spatial resolution is 2.5 metres.  The cameras are mounted on the satellite in such a
 way that near simultaneous imaging of the same area from two different angles is possible.  This facilitates the
 generation of accurate three-dimensional maps.  The cameras are steerable across the direction of the satellite’s
 movement to facilitate the imaging of an area more frequently.  The images taken by CARTOSAT-1 cameras are
 compressed, encrypted, formattedand transmitted to the ground stations.  The images are reconstructed from the data
 received at the ground stations. CARTOSAT-1also carries a Solid State Recorder with a capacity of 120 Giga Bits to
 store the images taken by its cameras.  The stored images can be transmitted when the satellite comes within the
 visibility zone of a ground station.
26.       Once commissioned, CARTOSAT-1 will give further fillip to remote sensing services by providing imagery
 with improved spatial resolution.  The unique high-resolution        along-track stereo imaging capability, carried out for
 the first time anywhere in the world, will enable generation of the Digital Elevation Models (DEM) and other value
 added products.  The date from CARTOSAT-1 is expected to provide enhanced inputs for large scale mapping
 applications and stimulate newer applications in the urban and rural development, land and water resources
 management, disaster assessment, relief planning and management, environment impact assessment and various other
 Geographical Information System applications.  The date can be used for updating topographic maps, besides
 generation of large-scale topographic maps.
27.       The Committee appreciates the role of space scientists and the Department of Space in devising the IRS system,
 which is the largest civilian remote sensing satellite constellation in the world. The Committee hopes that the
 Department would formulate plans to sell the imageries obtained from the IRS satellites, worldwide on a commercial
 basis on a larger scale, which would ensure generation of internal resources to fund future projects and popularization
 of  the achievements of the space scientists throughout the world.
HAMSAT
28.       HAMSAT is a microsatellite for providing satellite based Amateur Radio Services to the national as well as the
 international community of Amateur Radio Operators (HAMs).  Launched as an auxiliary payload along with
 CARTOSAT-1, the 42.5 kg HAMSAT will meet the long felt need of the Amateur Radio Operators in the South Asian
 region who possess the required equipment and operate in the UHF/VHF band based satellite radio communication. 
 One of the transponders of HAMSAT has been developed indigenously involving Indian HAMs, with the expertise of
 ISRO  and the experience of AMSAT-INDIA.  The second transponder the been developed by a Dutch Amateur Radio
 Operator and Graduate Engineering student at Higher Technical Institute, Venlo, The Netherlands.

29.       The Committee feels that HAMSAT is India’s contribution to the international community of Amateur Radio
 Operators and an effort to bring ISRO’s satellite services within the reach of the common man and popularise space
 technology among the masses. The Committee also feels that this satellite will play a valuable role in the national and
 international scenario by providing a low cost readily accessible and reliable means of communication during
 emergencies and calamities like floods, earthquakes, etc.  The Committee recommends that the Department should
 popularize the HAM Radio technology through seminars and organising demonstration programmes in the Universities,
 schools etc. to stimulate technical interest and awareness among the younger generation by providing them with an
 opportunity to develop their technological projects.
 EDUSAT
30.       The Committee has been informed that EDUSAT, launched on September 20, 2004, is the first Indian satellite
 built exclusively for serving the educational sector. It is mainly intended to meet the demand for an interactive satellite
 based distance education system for the country. It strongly reflects India’s commitment to use space technology for
 national development, especially for educating the population in remote and rural locations. The satellite was launched
 specially keeping in view the fact that the extension of quality education to remote and rural regions becomes a
 Herculean task for a large country like India with multi-lingual and multi-cultural population separated by vast
 geographical distances, and, in many instances, inaccessible terrain. Since independence, India has seen substantial
 increase in the number of educational institutions at primary, secondary and higher levels as well as the student
 enrolment but the lack of adequate rural educational infrastructure and non-availability of good teachers in sufficient
 numbers adversely affect the efforts made in education.
31.       On being asked whether there was any mechanism with the state Governments or the Ministry of Human
 Resource Development whereby the EDUSAT system could be provided on priority basis to the far flung areas where
 there was shortage of teachers and there were other difficulties and whether the Central or State Government would be
 competent to take such a decision, the Secretary of the Department clarified as follows:- 
“………. as far as the Tele-education is concerned, I would say that we have got five regional beams and one national
 beam.  The regional beams are meant for meeting the specific requirements of the States.  Here, basically, the users are
 the State governments and the State-based universities, whereas, the national beam are used by the agencies, such as
 All-India Council of Technical Education (AICTE), University Grants Commission(UGC) and Indira Gandhi National
 Open University(IGNOU).  They are all involved in planning.  We are constantly in dialogue with these people and are
 doing the needful.  There is also a National Committee with Prof. Dixit of IGNOU as the Chairman.  He has evaluated
 and appreciated the efforts and suggested taking up of such projects.  Then, the Ministry of Human Resource
 Development has informed that they have suggested to every State government are provided with a studio and fifty
 terminals, should further extend this to thousands of schools in the State.  And, of course, it is a State Subject.  The
 State Governments have to ask for funds and, I am sure, they would get it.  Some schools have asked that this be taken
 under the Sarva Siksha Abhiyan(SSA)  and they are getting funds under that.  So, it is spreading through such
 mechanisms.  But, the planning and intervention by the State agencies will take time.  There is a good coverage.  In
 almost all the States we have terminals in place and even recently we have set up one hub in Jammu and Kashmir.”
32.       The Committee is of the view that Satellites, such as the EDUSAT, can establish the connectivity between urban
 educational institutions with adequate infrastructure imparting quality education and the rural educational institutions
 that lack the necessary infrastructure. By doing so, we can help, to a considerable extent, in meeting the aspirations of
 the rural students. The Committee therefore, recommends that the Department of Space should formulate plans in
 coordination with the Ministry of Human Resource Development to spread education through the EDUSAT to all parts
 of the country.
VILLAGE RESOURCE CENTRES
 33.      Satellite based communication and remote sensing technologies have demonstrated their capabilities to provide
 services related to education, healthcare, weather, land and water resources management, mitigation of impact of
 natural disasters, etc. To provide these     space-based services directly to the rural areas, the Department has initiated a
 programme to set up Village Resource Centres (VRCs) in association with Non-Governmental Organisations(NGOs),
 trusts and state and central agencies concerned.  VRCs are envisaged as single window delivery mechanism for a
 variety of space based products and services, such as tele-education, tele-medicine, information on natural resources for
 planning and development at local level, interactive advisories on agriculture, fisheries, land and water resources
 management, livestock management, etc. interactive vocational training towards alternative livelihood, e-governance,
 weather information, etc.  VRCs will also address a variety of social aspects locally and can act as helplines. Housing,
 managing and operating the VRCs will rest with the associating agencies.  The department organises training of trainers
 on various aspects of VRCs for associating agencies like NGOs/ Trusts/ Institutions/ Government agencies; they in turn

34.       The first cluster of three VRCs was set up in Tamil Nadu.  During the year, the second cluster of nine VRCs has
 been set-up--six in Kerala and three in Tamilnadu (3). Efforts are on to identify villages, VRC locations and NGOs for

 & Nicobar Islands.
35.       The Committee feels that there is an urgent need to bridge the gap between the rural and urban population in
 terms of facilities available and the only means to accomplish the task is through technology. The concept of the
 Village Resource Centres (VRCs) is an excellent effort in this direction by the Department, which has the potential of
 transforming the socio-economic condition of rural India. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department
 should expedite its efforts towards establishing VRCs throughout the country, specially in the inaccessible and under-
developed regions of the country in a planned manner, so as to cover the entire country within a fixed period.
TELEMEDICINE
 
36.       The Committee has been apprised thatTelemedicine is one of the unique applications of space technology for
 societal benefit. The telemedicine programme, which started in 2001, is aimed at linking via INSAT remote/rural
 district hospitals in areas like Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh, Andaman and Lakshdweep Islands, North Eastern States
 and some of the remote and tribal districts in the States of Kerala, Kanataka, Tamil Nadu, Chhatisgarh, Punjab, West
 Bengal and Orissa with super-speciality hospitals in major cities.
37.       The Department provides the telemedicine systems- software, hardware and communication equipments as well
 as satellite bandwidth-the state governments and the speciality hospitals have to allocate funds for their part of
 infrastructure, manpower and maintenance. While Technology development, standards and cost effective systems have
 been evolved in association with various state Governments, NGOs, speciality hospitals and industry, the DOS interacts
 with state Governments and speciality hospitals for bringing an understanding between the parties through an
 Memorandum of Understanding (MOU).
38.       The Committee asked the Department whether central planning regarding                Tele-medicine should be
 made by the Health Ministry, in view of the fact that there is already a Task Force existing in the Ministry and whether
 the Department is also involved in it.      
    The Secretary of the Department clarified as follows:-
“Coming to the tele-medicine implementation, as you rightly pointed out, it is the responsibility of the health Ministry. 
 We already had three rounds of discussions with them.  We are also part of the basic system which is looking into the
 issue.  The mechanism of implementing the diagnostic data transfer technology will be made available to them and we
 will help the Health Ministry to take it up further.  A number of voluntary agencies have come forward to be part of the
 system which we are encouraging.  At some places, they will fund themselves totally.  At other places, we will give
 required equipment.  We are trying to target remote areas where the normal connectivity is not there.  For a cluster of
 villages, may be, about for 10.000 people there will be one centre.  Tele-medicine can be provided there."
39.       The Committee feels that in a developing country like India where due to scarcity of resources, the possibility of
 setting up of Hospitals and even primary health centres in the villages across the country, is not always possible;
 Telemedicine facilities provide an excellent alternative option to provide expert medical services to remote rural areas
 by linking hospitals/health centres in remote locations via satellites with specialty hospitals at major towns and cities.
 The Committee therefore recommends that the Department should carry on  its efforts  in coordination with Ministry of
 Health towards spreading the network of Tele-medicine centres in the rural areas lacking health care facilities.
40.       The Committee in its 144
th and 150th Reports had taken up the issue of development of a framework to tackle
 medico legal issues arising out of the development of Tele-medicine and recommended the evolution of such a
 framework at the earliest. The  Committee has been apprised by the Department that recommendations for initiating a
 framework for Medico- legal aspects of Telemedicine in the country has been submitted to the Department of Health
 for suitable formulation and  Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) is pursuing with Department of Health for
 further action in this matter.
41.       The Committee feels that the issue has been pending with the concerned Departments for quite some time now
 and needs to be expedited.  It, therefore, observes that the necessary framework for medico-legal aspects may be
 formulated at the earliest.  The Ministry of Law and Justice can also be consulted, if necessary.

44.       The Committee is constrained to note that the Department made budgetary provision for Navigational Satellite

utilisation of the budgetary provision of Rs. 350 crores in BE 2005-06.  Which was reduced to Rs. 10 crores in RE.  The
 Committee in this regard is of the opinion that necessary budgetary provision should be make by the Department only
 after a programme is finalized and approved by the competent authority.  Till then, the Department could make a taken
 provision in the budget against that programme.  Necessary provision can be made at the RE stage, in case the
 programme is finalized and approved by that time.  This is necessary for realistic budgeting.      
45.       The Secretary of the Department also apprised the Committee of the following facts pertaining to the Satellite
 Navigation:-
            “As far as technology development in the satellite area is concerned, as you have rightly observed, one of the
 major areas is satellite navigation.  Today the American GPS system is what is available globally.  People can use that
 for normal civilian applications, but there is no guarantee.  The only problem is that this GPS system is not a
 guaranteed system.  We cannot rely upon the signal all the time.  It is a limitation all over the world people have faced. 
 Even our Defence agencies have reported a number of times that the signal is distorted and they are not using it.  We
 need to  have an alternate system.  That is the reason we have taken up this alternate development activity.  We had
 some problem with the technology development.  Initially,  we did not know how to proceed.  After a lot of discussion
 with the International Agencies we have identified some sources where such development can be initiated.  With that
 confidence we have gone to the Cabinet and made a proposal for the Indian Regional Navigation System.  Here what
 we are proposing is, we will have seven satellites in our zone so that all Indian sub-continent and Indian Ocean Region
 will be covered by this system and that will provide accurate and guaranteed signal for all our security needs.  This
 development activity is supposed to be funded by us.  Because of the technical uncertainty, we did not commit anything
 major on this.  I am sure, at the Revised Estimate time, I will come with some definite funding requirement for this.”
46.       The Committee is happy to note that the Indian Space Scientists are proposing to develop indigenously, a
 complex technology, namely, Indian Regional navigation System.  The development of a reliable system by the Indian
 space Scientists will be another important achievement in this field especially in view of the fact that presently only the
 USA, GPS system is globally available for normal civilian applications and that to is not guaranteed and fully reliable.

 agency to provide space based services for the Disaster Management System of the country has been completed. During

 2004 in the States of Assam, Bihar, Meghalaya, Tripura and Arunachal Pradesh. Monitoring support for the Pareechu
 artificial lake formed in August 2004 in the Sutlej basin due to land slide and the associated flood hazard has been
 provided using satellite data.  Space services (Emergency Communications, Tele-medicine, Airborne survey and

49.       The Committee feels that the Department can help mitigating  the human and economic losses caused by
 disasters if the remote sensing data from the Earth Observation (EO) satellites were used more effectively in disaster
 management support in coordination with the local government agencies involved in relief work.  In addition to disaster
 management, the satellites can be used to detect, in the first place, the causes of the natural disasters like floods,

SUMMARY OF RECOMMENDATIONS
1.         The Committee commends the efforts of the Department in maintaining a record of more than 99% Budget
 utilisationduring the first three years of the Tenth Five Year Plan period, which points towards the fact that the
 Department has achieved most of the goals it had set for itself through proper planning and management of funds. The
 Committee hopes that the same pace of Budget utilisation would be maintained in the remaining two years of the Plan
 Period to ensure that all the long–term aims are realised.                      (Para 16)
2.         The Committee commends the role of the Indian space scientists in mastering a frontier space technology, which
 has brought the country close to the threshold of launching lunar spacecrafts and hopes that the technologies developed
 in this mission would be fully exploited in the future for embarking on planetary missions with well thought out
 scientific objectives. The Committee also hopes that the mission would expand the scientific knowledge about the
 origin and evolution of moon, upgrade India’s space technological capabilities and provide challenging opportunities to
 the young scientists working in planetary sciences.                                               (Para 20)
 
3.         The Committee appreciates the role of space scientists and the Department of Space in devising the IRS system,
 which is the largest civilian remote sensing satellite constellation in the world. The Committee hopes that the
 Department would formulate plans to sell the imageries obtained from the IRS satellites, worldwide on a commercial
 basis on a larger scale, which would ensure generation of internal resources to fund future projects and popularization
 of the achievements of the space scientists throughout the world.    (Para 27)
4.         The Committee feels that HAMSAT is India’s contribution to the international community of Amateur Radio
 Operators and an effort to bring ISRO’s satellite services within the reach of the common man and popularise space
 technology among the masses. The Committee also feels that this satellite will play a valuable role in the national and
 international scenario by providing a low cost readily accessible and reliable means of communication during
 emergencies and calamities like floods, earthquakes, etc.  The Committee recommends that the Department should
 popularize the HAM Radio technology through seminars and organising demonstration programmes in the Universities,
 schools etc. to stimulate technical interest and awareness among the younger generation by providing them with an
 opportunity to develop their technological projects.                          (Para 29)
 
5.         The Committee is of the view that Satellites, such as the EDUSAT, can establish the connectivity between urban
 educational institutions with adequate infrastructure imparting quality education and the rural educational institutions
 that lack the necessary infrastructure. By doing so, we can help, to a considerable extent, in meeting the aspirations of
 the rural students. The Committee therefore, recommends that the Department of Space should formulate plans in
 coordination with the Ministry of Human Resource Development to spread education through the EDUSAT to all parts
 of the country.                            (Para 32)

 terms of facilities available and the only means to accomplish the task is through technology. The concept of the
